doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

chapter: The music business and jazz education
title: Record jackets, losing the community audience, hip hop sampling
summary: Lost liner-note education, fewer black audiences at jazz clubs, and sampling versus analysing Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You know what I miss partly, that I think had something to with learning about people is reading the back of record jackets.
Somehow you got more connected to that artist because the whole, it was part of it. And thumbing through and you could stand in the store and read the back of it too you know.
And that was part of the educational process.

You see? So now you lose that connection, you lose these little subtleties that are sort of like the glue that holds all of these things together. And so it just becomes like this constant little thing that just happens over a period of time. It may be you know we have to think about reinventing the music in another kind of a way where — there’s something

about it I think when it became more like a cultural artsy kind of thing we lost that connection between the people. Sometimes those things can happen, you know, where I mean you go to like a jazz club now man, you’re not going to see as many black people as you saw like twenty, thirty years ago. You know what I’m saying is true. You go to concerts now, you know? I mean I’m just telling you the truth.

It’s just what it is so you’ve lost that connection with the community. You know? And we have to get back to introducing — it’s not foreign you know like some of the hip hop artists if you want to call them that, or acts or whatever you want to say. They know about it in a way because they sample it and they’re trying to figure it out. Because they’re not really creators of music they’re samplers of music. And that’s not a bad thing, I’m not trying to knock them but believe me they’re not trying to analyze a John Coltrane solo. They might like it and say I can use it in their own little way but they’re not trying to figure out, you know what I mean — “Giant Steps” or “Countdown,” — that’s not their thing. It’s what it is man.
